name: Lebanon
card_headline: Israel still holds a buffer zone in south Lebanon, the US-brokered framework is stalled, UNIFIL's mandate ends in December and parliament extended its own term
card_summary: Israel and Hezbollah have fought a new war since 2 March 2026. Lebanon's health ministry counted 4,324 dead by 13 July. Israel holds a buffer zone of about 5 to 6 percent of the country, and strikes continue after ceasefires in April and June. A US-brokered framework ties Israeli pullback to Hezbollah disarmament, which Hezbollah rejects, and the eighth round of talks is suspended. Parliament extended its own term by two years. The World Bank projects GDP will fall 6.4 percent in 2026.
card_local: L'Orient Today relays the health ministry's death tolls, the justice minister's claim that disarmament will happen and the IMF talks, and Annahar tracks Syrian refugee returns. [11][16][19][20]
card_international: NPR, Al Jazeera, Arab News and The National report the framework, the suspended talks and the 16 November visit of US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz. [1][6][7][8]
card_scholar: ACLED finds violence at its highest since October 2023 and strikes rising after the June ceasefire, and Carnegie's Michael Young argues against forcibly disarming Hezbollah. [9][12]
context_md: Lebanon defaulted on its debt for the first time in March 2020, and the financial collapse had begun in 2019. [18][4] A port explosion on 4 August 2020 killed more than 200 people. [17] A US- and France-brokered ceasefire took effect in November 2024 after more than a year of fighting that killed most of Hezbollah's leadership, including Hassan Nasrallah. [4] Joseph Aoun, who led the army from 2017, became president in January 2025. [4] The UN Security Council voted in August 2025 to end UNIFIL at the end of 2026. [24] The current war followed the start of US-Israeli military operations against Iran on 28 February 2026. [4] Parliament extended its own term in March, so elections planned for May did not take place. [2]

sections.title: Israel holds a buffer zone in the south and strikes have continued through two ceasefires
sections.body_md:
The current war began on 2 March 2026. The Congressional Research Service says Hezbollah resumed firing into Israel after US-Israeli military operations against Iran began on 28 February, and that Israel then expanded its ground operations and set up a buffer zone covering about 5 percent of Lebanon. [4] ACLED puts the Israeli-controlled area at around 6 percent. [9] The National reported that Hezbollah attacked Israel after Iran's supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed, and that Israel responded with a new offensive. [2]

Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health counted 4,324 people killed and 12,224 injured as of 13 July, including 253 children and 135 health workers killed on duty. [5] Earlier ministry figures reported by L'Orient Today gave 3,185 killed by 25 May. [11] These are the ministry's counts. Israeli figures on militants killed were not found in the sources read for this draft.

Two ceasefires have not ended the strikes. Donald Trump announced a ten-day ceasefire on 16 April and said Israel was prohibited from bombing Lebanon, while Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was staying. [1] L'Orient Today reports that the truce was extended twice and did not stop Israeli strikes in the south and the Bekaa, or Hezbollah attacks on Israeli forces. [11] OCHA records a further ceasefire announcement on 20 June and says 344 people were killed after it by 13 July. [5] ACLED dates that ceasefire to 21 June. It finds air and drone strikes have risen since, with September the highest month, and that 73 percent of property-destruction events recorded since March happened after it. [9]

The pattern continues in November. Arab News reported Israeli demolitions and shelling in villages inside or beside the Israeli-held zone on 9 November. [7] An aggregator that maps events from Lebanese and Israeli media records strikes in Nabatieh and Bint Jbeil districts through 24 November, along with Israeli military statements about tunnels and weapons caches destroyed. This draft could not verify those statements independently. [15]

lenses.local: L'Orient Today carries the health ministry's running death toll for strikes since 2 March. [11]
lenses.international: NPR reports the April ceasefire and Israel's stated intent to stay, and Al Jazeera reports strikes continuing after the June framework. [1][6]
lenses.scholar: ACLED finds violence at its highest since October 2023 and strikes rising after the June ceasefire. [9]

sections.title: The June framework ties Israeli pullback to Hezbollah disarmament, and talks are suspended
sections.body_md:
The framework was signed on 26 June at the US State Department after four days of talks. The signatories were State Department Counselor Daniel Holler, Israeli ambassador Yechiel Leiter and Lebanese ambassador Nada Hamadeh, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio attending. [6] It sets a sequenced process in which the Lebanese army restores authority over all territory as armed groups are verifiably disarmed. Israel would progressively redeploy and hand two pilot zones to the army, one south of the Litani and one north. It does not require an Israeli withdrawal. [6]

Reactions split. Netanyahu said Israeli forces will hold the buffer zone until Hezbollah disarms. President Joseph Aoun welcomed the deal as a first step toward sovereignty. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem called it “null and void.” [6] CRS reports that Hezbollah's leader rejected it as a surrender of sovereignty. [4]

Arab News reported on 9 November that the eighth round of direct talks had been suspended, with disputes over Israeli withdrawal, implementation of the framework and a verification mechanism. [7] Hezbollah MP Ali Fayyad said US election results would not change the party's position, which includes a right to resist. [7] Army commander Rodolphe Haykal called the continued Israeli presence the main problem facing the country. [7] Aoun said in July that the presence prevents the army from deploying in the south. [4] The WarHistory aggregator reports that Aoun said on 24 November the talks were on hold because of Israeli elections. That rests on one aggregator and is unconfirmed. [15]

Inside Lebanon the argument is over method. The government formally banned Hezbollah's military activities, which CRS calls unprecedented but largely symbolic. Hezbollah holds 13 of 128 parliamentary seats and has refused to disarm. [4] Justice Minister Adel Nassar, whose seat belongs to the Kataeb party, said disarmament “will take place.” [16] Carnegie's Michael Young argues against using force and warns of civil conflict, citing the army commander's priority of “preventing civil war.” [12] In June Young described an Egyptian-initiated plan, shared with Hezbollah and Israel, for phased integration of Hezbollah members into state institutions. [13] Crisis Group urged in 2025 that Israeli withdrawal be sequenced in steps against Lebanese disarmament milestones. [14]

lenses.local: L'Orient Today reports Justice Minister Nassar's statement that disarmament is settled, which is an official's claim. [16]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, Arab News and The National report the framework terms, Hezbollah's rejection and the suspended talks. [6][7][8]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Young argues against forced disarmament, and Crisis Group proposed reciprocal sequencing in 2025. [12][14]

sections.title: UNIFIL's mandate ends in December and no successor is agreed
sections.body_md:
The UN Security Council voted in August 2025 to end UNIFIL's mandate at the end of 2026, after which the force has one year to wrap up and withdraw. About 7,500 peacekeepers from 46 countries are deployed, down from a peak near 10,000. [24] UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix said no decision had been made on what UN presence, if any, would follow. The EU plans a support mission to train the Lebanese army, not to patrol the border. [24]

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, visited Beirut on 16 November and met Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Speaker Nabih Berri. He said Washington has no interest in preserving the current mission, and France is expected to draft a Security Council proposal. [8] Rubio has said the successor “could be a civilian mission” that helps verify Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah disarmament. [8] Salam wants a Council-mandated presence for monitoring and support to the army. Israel has rejected the multinational ground force Lebanon proposed. [8]

The peacekeepers' record is part of the dispute. NPR reported that after the 2024 ceasefire UN peacekeepers logged more than 10,000 violations, nearly all by Israel. [1] Aoun said that withdrawing the force would create a vacuum. [24] The AP report lists open questions: who escorts aid convoys in the Israeli-occupied area, and who fills the liaison role that prevents clashes between Israeli and Lebanese troops. [24]

lenses.international: AP reports the UN peacekeeping chief's warning of open questions, and The National reports Waltz's visit and the US position. [24][8]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Maha Yahya, on a November podcast, argues that Lebanon's future could signal the direction of the wider international order. [25]

sections.title: Parliament extended its own term by two years during the war
sections.body_md:
Parliament voted 76 to 41, with four abstentions, on 9 March to extend its own mandate by two years. The vote postponed elections that had been scheduled for May. [2][3] The session took place during Israeli strikes and mass displacement. [3] The National does not say who proposed the motion. [2] Gebran Bassil, head of the Free Patriotic Movement, called it “a betrayal of the public trust” and said it could be challenged before the Constitutional Council. [2]

Carnegie's Issam Kayssi reports that Christian parties accepted a delay but proposed shorter ones, from two months to a year, and that Melhem Khalaf called the two-year term unconstitutional. [3] Independent MP Firas Hamdan said organising elections would take at least nine or ten months given the displacement. [3] The next parliament will elect the next president. [3] The National notes that the last elections, in May 2022, had low turnout, and that Hezbollah and its allies lost their majority. [2]

The state's other open file is the Beirut port explosion of 4 August 2020, which killed more than 200 people. [17] Judge Tarek Bitar closed his investigation on 30 March and sent the file to the Court of Cassation prosecutor, who returned his submission on 15 September. [16] A senior judicial official told Reuters that Bitar's report accuses 70 people. [17] Nassar says an indictment is expected before the end of the year. No indictment had been issued as of the latest source read. [16][17] Reuters reports that years of political interference and legal challenges stalled the probe. [17]

lenses.local: L'Orient Today carries the Justice Minister's statement on the port blast indictment, an official's claim not independently verified. [16]
lenses.international: The National and Reuters report the extension vote and the state of the port blast case. [2][17]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Kayssi sets the extension against Lebanon's history of wartime postponements and records the objections of Christian parties. [3]

sections.title: The economy is set to shrink 6.4 percent as the IMF waits on two banking laws
sections.body_md:
The World Bank's Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor projects real GDP will contract 6.4 percent in 2026. That reverses a 2025 recovery of 4.2 percent, the fastest since the 2019 crisis began. It expects inflation of 17.5 percent, calls public debt unsustainable and says debt restructuring negotiations have not begun. [21] CRS gives 2025 growth as 3.5 percent and says nominal GDP fell from nearly $55 billion in 2018 to under $20 billion in 2021. [4] The two sources disagree on 2025, and this draft does not reconcile them.

The Bank says housing and infrastructure damage, displacement and supply-chain disruption weigh on output, and that tourism and domestic demand fell. [21] CRS notes the 2024 conflict cost $7.2 billion in economic losses and $6.8 billion in physical damage. [4] This draft found no 2026 damage estimate. Israel has named Hezbollah's financial arm, Al Qard Al Hassan, as a target. [2]

An IMF mission visited from 11 to 13 November. Mission chief Ernesto Ramirez Rigo said further work is needed to agree a strategy for restructuring the banking sector. [18] The IMF calls the Bank Resolution Law and the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law, known as the financial gap law, essential once adopted, and says the financial gap law should keep the hierarchy of claims. [18] The National puts losses from the financial collapse at roughly $70 billion, a figure used since 2022 that it says is now expected to be higher. [18] Parliament passed a bank resolution law in August, and Aoun appealed it to the Constitutional Council over an amendment on central bank independence and powers. [18] L'Orient Today reported that at the IMF Spring Meetings no agreement was reached and talks centred on that law, the draft financial gap law and a medium-term fiscal framework. [19] The 2022 staff-level agreement remains unimplemented. [4]

lenses.local: L'Orient Today reports that the Spring Meetings ended without an agreement on the banking laws or the fiscal framework. [19]
lenses.international: The National reports the IMF's November mission and the unresolved bank resolution law. [18]
lenses.scholar: The World Bank projects a 6.4 percent contraction in 2026 and calls debt unsustainable. [21]

sections.title: About 412,700 people were still displaced in July and the flash appeal was under half funded
sections.body_md:
OCHA's Flash Update 44 puts the number still displaced at about 412,700 as of 15 July. It counts 741,111 people returned to their areas of origin, with returns slowing to about 8,500 over eight days, and about 30,500 people in 292 collective shelters. [5] At the peak, NPR reported that roughly a fifth of the population, more than a million people, was displaced, and that Lebanese officials say Israel has demolished more than 40,000 homes in the south. [1]

The 2026 Flash Appeal had received $284.8 million, or 44.5 percent of the $639.9 million requested for six months, as of 16 July. [5] Access is unpredictable in the South and Nabatieh governorates. The share of movement notifications receiving negative responses rose to 11 percent from 1 percent, and unexploded ordnance, damaged roads and GPS spoofing slow deliveries. [5]

Lebanon also hosts Syrian refugees. Annahar cites UNHCR for about 507,000 registered Syrian refugees in early 2026 and more than 609,000 returns to Syria between 8 December 2024 and the end of April 2026. UNHCR reports no sharp decrease in the refugee population after the March war. [20] Syrian authorities counted about 200,000 crossings into Syria between 2 and 27 March, while IOM counted 120,727 entries from 2 March to 1 June. [20] A private study cited by Annahar puts the Syrians remaining at 800,000 to 900,000, far above the registered count, and the article does not explain the gap. [20]

lenses.local: Annahar reports the UNHCR, IOM and Syrian government figures on returns and shows how far they differ. [20]
lenses.international: NPR reports that more than a million people were displaced at the peak. [1]
lenses.scholar: OCHA's update says displacement may be beginning to stabilize while access and funding remain constrained. [5]

sections.title: Four journalists were killed in 2026 and no prosecutions have followed
sections.body_md:
CPJ researchers Rama Sabanekh and Nader Durgham name four journalists killed in Lebanon in 2026: Ali Shoaib, Fatima Ftouni and Mohammed Ftouni in Jezzine in March, and Amal Khalil in Bint Jbeil about a month later. [22] CPJ says no criminal prosecution has followed attacks on journalists since 2023. It reports that Israel acknowledged in 2026 that its forces fired the tank rounds in the 13 October 2023 attack that killed Issam Abdallah, but described it as a mistake. It also says Israeli forces obstructed medical workers from reaching the site of Khalil's killing for hours. [22]

Lebanon withdrew its 2024 declaration accepting ICC jurisdiction, and CPJ says the 2026 framework raises concerns that it could obstruct accountability. [22] Journalists told CPJ that parts of the south are inaccessible because of the Israeli presence and the risk of being targeted, and that some have hidden their press gear. [22]

Human Rights Watch says the Israeli military used white phosphorus over homes in Yohmor on 3 March and calls airburst use over populated areas unlawful. The Israeli military told Reuters it was unaware of and could not confirm the use of white phosphorus, and Reuters could not verify HRW's findings. [23] The aggregator WarHistory reports that the government is documenting Israeli attacks for possible legal action, a single-sourced item. [15]

lenses.local: No Lebanese outlet's reporting on press freedom was read directly for this draft.
lenses.international: CPJ and HRW document attacks on journalists and the use of white phosphorus, and Israel disputes or could not confirm parts of that. [22][23]
lenses.scholar: CPJ cites several independent investigations that concluded clearly identifiable journalists were deliberately targeted, including in October 2023. [22]

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: L'Orient Today and Annahar were read through single articles, and NNA, LBCI, Naharnet, Al-Akhbar and Hezbollah-aligned outlets such as Al-Manar were not read directly.
Israeli government and military statements were read only second hand (NPR, Al Jazeera, an aggregator). No Hezbollah statement was read directly.

The latest death toll found is the health ministry's 4,324 as of 13 July via OCHA. Other figures in the sources differ in date and basis (CRS about 4,300, Al Jazeera 4,192 at 27 June). Nothing later was found.
The 24 November report that talks are on hold because of Israeli elections rests on one aggregator (WarHistory), as do the November IDF claims and the arrest of five Hezbollah members.

Source figures conflict and were not reconciled: buffer zone about 5 percent (CRS) against about 6 percent (ACLED), 2025 growth 3.5 percent (CRS) against 4.2 percent (World Bank), and ceasefire dates of 20 June (OCHA) against 21 June (ACLED).
The IMF and World Bank documents were read through a press release and press reports, not the full texts. No 2026 damage or reconstruction estimate was found.
The UNIFIL article from AP has no calendar date. The L'Orient Today IMF piece and the Nassar piece have inferred dates.

The Iran war context (28 February US-Israeli operations, the killing of Khamenei) rests on CRS and The National and was not researched further. Gulf and Iranian funding of Hezbollah, Palestinian camps, emigration, and sectarian politics beyond the Shia and Christian parties are thin or absent.
No Freedom House or RSF press-freedom index was read, and no Lebanese rights group other than through CPJ and HRW.
Book entries were verified through bookseller, review and list pages, and none is from 2025 or 2026. Podcast and film links point to listing pages.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP, AFP and NPR file on Lebanon regularly when strikes, ceasefires or talks make news [1][17][24]. ACLED, OCHA and Carnegie publish steady analysis, and L'Orient Today and Annahar report daily [9][5][12][11][20]. The economic and rights files are covered less than the fighting [18][22].

severity.basis: The health ministry counted 4,324 killed by 13 July, and ACLED recorded the highest violence since October 2023 with strikes rising after the June ceasefire [5][9].
About 412,700 people were still displaced in July and the flash appeal was 44.5 percent funded [5].
Parliament extended its own term by two years and CPJ names four journalists killed in 2026 with no prosecutions [3][22].
The World Bank projects a 6.4 percent contraction and 17.5 percent inflation, calls debt unsustainable and says restructuring talks have not begun [21].
The June framework is stalled with talks suspended, strikes rose after the June ceasefire, and OCHA says displacement may be beginning to stabilize [7][9][5].

parts.basis: The US brokered the framework and Rubio attended the signing, France is expected to draft a UN proposal, and Iran has tied a Lebanon ceasefire to its own with Washington [6][8][13].
Nominal GDP fell from nearly $55 billion in 2018 to under $20 billion in 2021, so Lebanon's weight in world trade is small [4].
This round began inside a regional war involving Iran, and about 200,000 people crossed into Syria in March according to Syrian authorities [2][20].
Lebanon hosts about 507,000 registered Syrian refugees and returns across the border continue [20].
UNIFIL, in place since 1978, is ending without a successor, and Lebanon withdrew its ICC declaration while CPJ questions accountability under the framework [8][22].

summary: Lebanon matters beyond its borders because the Israel-Hezbollah front is tied to the US-Iran track and because the end of UNIFIL removes a long-standing monitoring force [13][8]. Its economy is too small to carry global weight [4].
gi.up: Renewed large-scale Israeli ground operations north of the Litani, a collapse of the US-Iran talks, or armed clashes between the army and Hezbollah.
gi.down: Verified Israeli withdrawal from the pilot zones, a functioning successor to UNIFIL and a Hezbollah handover of heavy weapons.
